newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich gets boost from China trip.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich gets boost from China trip.

text.p: Many a politician has found diplomatic globe-trotting a relief from controversy back home, and Newt Gingrich's China trip is a strong case in point.

In Hong Kong, Beijing and Taipei, Gingrich, speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, burnished his image with Americans -- even if he did not quell disgruntlement among fellow House Republicans -- by delivering a blunt message to China's leaders on human rights and political freedoms.
It was his most visible public outing since the House voted in January to reprimand him for ethics violations and he agreed to pay a $300,000 penalty -- still outstanding.

Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, received generally higher grades in editorial page reviews than did Democratic Vice President Al Gore, who was in the same area at about the same time and took a conciliatory stance on his visit to Beijing.

Gingrich's comments about China's record on human rights abuses and suppression of dissent were "refreshingly candid" and "in some ways more honest than Mr. Gore's anaemic formulations," the New York Times said.

The Wall Street Journal praised the speaker, who was leading a bipartisan delegation, for giving "the kind of nuanced, confident, professional performance Americans ought to expect of their political leaders in dealing with foreign countries."
But Gingrich's emergence on the international stage masked deepening political troubles at home.
He is under pressure to decide how he will pay the $300,000 penalty. His spokesman says he plans no decision until this summer after all options are fully researched.

He has meantime incurred the wrath of conservatives in his party -- once the very core of his power base -- for apparent willingness to hold off on a planned tax cut, the "crown jewel" of the Republican agenda, until other elements of a balanced budget deal are nailed down.
The ethics front has been quiet. The House ethics committee has imposed a moratorium on new complaints while it awaits the recommendations of a task force considering reforms in procedures.
The moratorium ends on April 11 and it is not yet clear whether a new committee will proceed on a still-pending ethics charge filed against by Democrats.

House Republicans are also restive over a seeming lack of direction and inability to point to any real accomplishments since the new Congress convened in January. House leaders suffered a setback when deficit-minded Republican rebels defeated a commiteee spending measure.

Congress returns to work next week after a two-week recess but there is little hope negotiations on a balanced budget deal with the White House will produce agreement by the April 15 deadline for writing the budget for the 1998 fiscal year.

All of these problems have turned Gingrich, once hailed as the architect of the 1994 election victory that produced the first Republican Congress in 40 years, into a lightning rod for his troops' discontent.

So far this unhappiness has not burst out into open revolt against Gingrich. When one outspoken Republican, Representative Peter King of New York, recently went so far as to call the speaker "political road kill," Gingrich ally Gerald Solomon of New York leapt to the defence of "our visionary leader."
"Republicans high and low are quietly saying that it's only a matter of time until Gingrich is gone," political commentator Charles Cook wrote in the congressional newspaper Roll Call.
Cook said Gingrich's best chance was to persuade his Republican critics to lay off while sending a quiet message that he would step down when the current Congress concludes at the end of next year.
But Cook questioned whether Gingrich could last that long, adding, "Today, the smart money says he can't."
